questions.question: An offline-first notes app shows a list that must work on a plane and update when the network returns. What should the list screen observe?
options: A query on the local database (Room / Core Data or SwiftData) that the sync layer writes network results into
Whichever of the network call or the database read completes first, then ignore the other
An in-memory cache held by the ViewModel that is refilled from the API on every screen open
The latest network response, falling back to a database read only when the request fails
questions.explanation: With a single source of truth the UI only observes the local store, and the network layer's job is to update that store; the screen then re-renders automatically from the DB query. Falling back to the DB only on failure gives two competing sources, so data can flicker or disagree between screens. An in-memory cache disappears on process death and does not work offline after a restart.

questions.question: With cache-then-network, a screen can render twice (cached data first, fresh data second), so the UI must tolerate content changing under the user, for example by keeping scroll position and not resetting inputs.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Cache-then-network shows stored data instantly and then replaces it when the refresh lands, so the same screen renders at least twice. If the list resets its scroll or a text field is rebuilt on the second render, users see a jump. Stable item keys and a diffing list keep the update smooth.

questions.question: A user taps 'Like' on a post while offline. Which design keeps the like and still delivers it later?
options: Keep the pending like in the ViewModel and resend it from onResume / sceneWillEnterForeground when the app returns
Disable the Like button while offline and show a snackbar asking the user to retry once they reconnect
Write the like to the local DB plus a pending-operations (outbox) table, show it at once, and drain the outbox from WorkManager / BGTaskScheduler when online
Send the request straight away with an OkHttp / URLSession retry policy that keeps retrying until it succeeds
questions.explanation: An outbox stored on disk survives process death and app restarts, and a scheduled job with a network constraint delivers it when connectivity returns. Holding it in the ViewModel loses it as soon as the process is killed. An in-flight HTTP retry also dies with the process and does nothing for a user who is offline for hours.

questions.question: Your outbox retries 'place order' after a socket timeout, and support sees duplicate orders. The first request had actually reached the server. What is the right fix?
options: Add exponential backoff with jitter so the retry reaches the server only after the first request has finished
Generate a fresh request ID on each retry so the server can log every attempt and drop the extra orders later
Stop retrying on timeouts and only retry on 5xx responses, since a timeout usually means the order went through
Generate a UUID idempotency key when the operation is created, store it with the outbox row, send it on every retry, and let the server dedupe on it
questions.explanation: A timeout is ambiguous: the client cannot know whether the server processed the request, so the only safe retry is one the server can recognise as a repeat. The key must be created once per logical operation and persisted, otherwise a retry after process death gets a new key. Backoff changes timing but not the duplicate, and skipping retries on timeouts just loses orders instead.

questions.question: You show a sent comment immediately (optimistic UI) before the server confirms it. Which pieces do you need for this to be robust? Select all that apply.
options: A per-row sync state (pending / sent / failed) so the UI can show 'sending' and offer retry
Deleting the local row before the request is sent so a server echo of the comment cannot appear twice
Disabling pull-to-refresh until every pending write is confirmed so a refresh cannot overwrite them
Mapping the client's temporary ID to the server-assigned ID when the ack arrives, without duplicating the row
A way to roll back or mark the row failed when the server rejects the write (e.g. validation or 403)
questions.explanation: Optimistic UI is a promise you may have to take back, so the row needs a visible state, a failure path and a clean reconciliation with the server's ID. Blocking refresh is not needed if the merge keeps pending rows when applying server data. Deleting the local row first defeats the whole point of showing it instantly.

questions.question: Two phones edit the same note offline. On sync you resolve with last-write-wins using each device's local timestamp. What is the main risk?
options: Last-write-wins needs vector clocks to work at all, so device timestamps would make every sync fail outright
Clock skew can make the older edit 'win', and the losing edit is dropped silently with no trace for the user
The server rejects both writes as conflicting and the note is left at its version from before either edit
Both edits are merged character by character, which can leave the note with text from both devices in it
questions.explanation: LWW throws away one side of a conflict by design, and with device clocks the 'later' write may simply be the phone with the fast clock. That is acceptable for things like a profile photo but bad for user-authored text. LWW never merges; merging needs a field-level or CRDT-style strategy, or a 'conflict copy' shown to the user.

questions.question: If a client sends `If-Match` with the ETag it last saw, and the server's current ETag for that resource is different, the server should apply the write anyway and return the newer ETag.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: `If-Match` makes the write conditional: if the resource changed since the client read it, the server should refuse with 412 Precondition Failed. The client then fetches the latest version and rebases or asks the user. Applying it anyway is exactly the silent overwrite that optimistic concurrency control exists to prevent.

questions.question: Your sync engine attaches a version vector (one counter per device) to each record. When two versions arrive, what does comparing the vectors tell you?
options: A total order across all devices, so the record with the larger vector sum is always the correct winner
Whether one version causally follows the other or they are concurrent, but not which concurrent edit should win
The same thing as last-write-wins, except that it uses logical counters instead of wall-clock timestamps
That the server is no longer needed, because devices can now agree on the winner without any merge logic
questions.explanation: If every counter in A is ≤ B's, A happened before B and B can replace it; if each has a counter the other lacks, the edits are concurrent and you must merge or surface a conflict. Version vectors detect conflicts; they do not decide them. Summing the counters invents an order that does not exist and quietly turns into LWW.

questions.question: A shared shopping list is edited offline by several family members. Which techniques help concurrent edits converge without losing data? Select all that apply.
options: Hard-delete rows on the device immediately, because the next full download will remove them everywhere
Model quantity changes as per-device increments that are summed, so concurrent '+1's add up instead of overwriting
Resolve per field (title, checked, quantity) rather than per row, so edits to different fields both survive
Keep deleted items as tombstones (e.g. a deleted flag plus version) so a delete is synced instead of looking like a missing row
Store the whole list as one JSON blob resolved with last-write-wins, so the newest full copy always replaces the rest
questions.explanation: Tombstones, field-level registers and counter CRDTs are the practical 'CRDT-lite' tools most apps use. One blob with LWW drops every concurrent change except one. Hard-deleting locally without a tombstone means another device's copy can resurrect the item, and the delete is never propagated.

questions.question: A field-service app holds 50k records and needs fast incremental sync that also handles deletes. Which design is the most reliable?
options: The client asks for rows where `updated_at > lastSyncTime`, using the device clock time of the previous successful sync
The client downloads the full dataset every night via a periodic job and replaces the local tables in a single swap
The server exposes a change feed keyed by an opaque sync token; the client applies upserts and tombstones and saves the new token in the same DB transaction
The server pushes every changed record inside FCM / APNs payloads, and the client writes each payload into its DB
questions.explanation: A server-issued token avoids clock skew, tombstones carry deletes, and committing the token with the data means a crash can never mark changes as synced that were not stored. `updated_at` against the device clock misses rows when clocks disagree and never sees deleted rows at all. Push payloads are size-limited and not guaranteed, so they work as a 'sync now' hint, not as the data channel.
